title: English Test 1
subject: English
description: SSC CGL Tier 2 expected questions: Synonyms, Antonyms, One Word Substitution, Spelling Correction, Error Detection, and Reading Comprehension.

questions.q: Choose the word that is most similar in meaning to the given word: AGGRANDIZE
questions.why: Aggrandize means to increase the power, status, or wealth of someone/something. 'Ennoble' is its closest synonym.

questions.q: Choose the word that is most similar in meaning to the given word: ACERBIC
questions.why: Acerbic means sharp, sarcastic, and direct in speaking. 'Sardonic' (grimly mocking or cynical) is the best synonym.

questions.q: Choose the word that is most similar in meaning to the given word: ABNEGATE
questions.why: Abnegate means to renounce or reject a desired right or responsibility. 'Relinquish' means to voluntarily cease to keep or claim.

questions.q: Choose the word that is most similar in meaning to the given word: AMELIORATE
questions.why: Ameliorate means to make something bad or unsatisfactory better. 'Mitigate' means to make less severe or painful.

questions.q: Choose the word that is opposite in meaning to the given word: ASCETIC
questions.why: Ascetic means characterized by severe self-discipline and abstention. 'Sybaritic' means fond of luxury and pleasure, making it the perfect antonym.

questions.q: Choose the word that is opposite in meaning to the given word: AMENABLE
questions.why: Amenable means easily persuaded or controlled. 'Recalcitrant' means having an obstinately uncooperative attitude toward authority.

questions.q: Choose the word that is opposite in meaning to the given word: ANIMOSITY
questions.why: Animosity means strong hostility. 'Rapport' means a close and harmonious relationship, acting as its antonym.

questions.q: Choose the word that is opposite in meaning to the given word: ARCHAIC
questions.why: Archaic means very old or old-fashioned. 'Contemporary' means modern or living/occurring at the same time.

questions.q: Select the correct One Word Substitution: A person who completely abandons his religious or political beliefs.
questions.why: An Apostate is someone who forsakes their religion, cause, or political party.

questions.q: Select the correct One Word Substitution: Loss of ability to understand or express speech, caused by brain damage.
questions.why: Aphasia is a language disorder that affects a person's ability to communicate. (Amnesia is memory loss; Anorexia is an eating disorder).

questions.q: Select the correct One Word Substitution: An extensive group of islands.
questions.why: An archipelago is a sea or stretch of water containing many islands.

questions.q: Select the correct One Word Substitution: A place where animals are slaughtered for consumption.
questions.why: An abattoir is a slaughterhouse. (An apiary is where bees are kept; an arsenal is for weapons).

questions.q: Select the correct One Word Substitution: Able to use both hands with equal skill.
questions.why: Ambidextrous refers to a person who can use their right and left hands equally well.

questions.q: Choose the correctly spelt word from the following options:
questions.why: The correct spelling is 'Annihilate', which means to destroy utterly or obliterate.

questions.q: Choose the correctly spelt word from the following options:
questions.why: The correct spelling is 'Amateur', which refers to a person who engages in a pursuit on an unpaid basis.

questions.q: Identify the segment which contains a grammatical error: Every of the board members (A) / was completely against the (B) / newly proposed corporate policies. (C) / No error (D)
questions.why: 'Every' functions only as an Adjective, never as a pronoun. We cannot say 'Every of X'. It must be 'Each of the board members'.

questions.q: Identify the segment which contains a grammatical error: The defense attorney gave the jury (A) / each reason to doubt (B) / the authenticity of the prime witness. (C) / No error (D)
opts: The defense attorney gave the jury
the authenticity of the prime witness
questions.why: 'Each' cannot be used with an Abstract Noun. 'Reason' is an abstract noun, so it must be 'every reason'.

questions.q: Identify the segment which contains a grammatical error: During the press conference, both the CEO (A) / as well as the Managing Director (B) / refused to answer the allegations. (C) / No error (D)
opts: During the press conference, both the CEO
as well as the Managing Director
questions.ansText: as well as the Managing Director
questions.why: The conjunction 'Both' is never followed by 'as well as'. It is strictly paired with 'and' (Both ... and).

questions.q: Identify the segment which contains a grammatical error: Despite having valid tickets, (A) / both the passengers are not (B) / allowed to board the international flight. (C) / No error (D)
opts: allowed to board the international flight
questions.why: 'Both' is never used in a negative sentence (with 'not'). We must replace it with 'Neither of the passengers is'.

questions.q: Identify the segment which contains a grammatical error: My both students have qualified (A) / for the final round of the (B) / prestigious national debate competition. (C) / No error (D)
opts: for the final round of the
questions.why: Possessive Adjectives (My, his, her, their) must always come after 'Both', not before it. It should be 'Both my students'.

questions.q: Identify the segment which contains a grammatical error: The detective realized that this is (A) / the same mysterious man who (B) / had been loitering near the vault. (C) / No error (D)
opts: The detective realized that this is
had been loitering near the vault
questions.why: Phrases containing 'the same' must ALWAYS be followed by the relative pronoun 'that'. It should be 'the same mysterious man that'.

questions.q: Identify the segment which contains a grammatical error: There was absolutely nothing in the report (A) / which could prove that the suspect (B) / was present at the crime scene. (C) / No error (D)
opts: There was absolutely nothing in the report
which could prove that the suspect
was present at the crime scene
questions.ansText: which could prove that the suspect
questions.why: Words like 'nothing', 'anything', and 'something' are strictly followed by 'that', not 'which'. It should be 'nothing in the report that'.

questions.q: Identify the segment which contains a grammatical error: The management has decided to promote (A) / whomever successfully completes (B) / the rigorous training program. (C) / No error (D)
opts: The management has decided to promote
questions.why: The verb 'completes' requires a subject, so the subjective case 'whoever' must be used instead of the objective 'whomever'.

questions.q: Identify the segment which contains a grammatical error: If the organization had sufficient funds, (A) / they would have invested heavily (B) / in the new artificial intelligence project. (C) / No error (D)
opts: If the organization had sufficient funds,
in the new artificial intelligence project
questions.why: 'Had' alone is Simple Past (V2). The result clause for V2 must be 'would + V1'. It should be 'they would invest'.

questions.q: Identify the segment which contains a grammatical error: If you continuously heat water to 100 degrees, (A) / it will turn into vapor (B) / within a few minutes. (C) / No error (D)
opts: If you continuously heat water to 100 degrees,
questions.why: Universal truths take Simple Present tense in both clauses. It should be 'it turns into vapor' instead of 'it will turn'.

questions.q: Identify the segment which contains a grammatical error: One of the greatest desires of the (A) / citizens living in the valley are (B) / to have a well-functioning hospital. (C) / No error (D)
opts: One of the greatest desires of the
citizens living in the valley are
questions.ansText: citizens living in the valley are
questions.why: The structure 'One of the + Plural Noun' takes a Singular Verb. 'Are' must be replaced with 'is' to agree with 'One'.

questions.q: Identify the segment which contains a grammatical error: Sneha is definitely one of the girls (A) / who always thinks creatively (B) / during the crucial brainstorming sessions. (C) / No error (D)
opts: Sneha is definitely one of the girls
questions.why: 'One of the + Plural Noun + Who/Which/That' requires a Plural Verb to agree with the plural antecedent (girls). It should be 'who always think'.

questions.q: Identify the segment which contains a grammatical error: The manager noted that Rahul is only one (A) / of the employees who have consistently (B) / met their sales targets this year. (C) / No error (D)
opts: The manager noted that Rahul is only one
of the employees who have consistently
met their sales targets this year
questions.ansText: of the employees who have consistently
questions.why: The specific structure 'ONLY one of the + Plural Noun + Who' forces the verb to be Singular. It should be 'who has', not 'who have'.

questions.q: Identify the segment which contains a grammatical error: Each of the students selected for the program (A) / is preparing extremely hard (B) / to clear their final examinations. (C) / No error (D)
opts: Each of the students selected for the program
questions.why: 'Each of' is followed by a Singular Adjective/Pronoun. 'Their' is plural and must be replaced with the singular 'his'.

questions.q: Identify the segment which contains a grammatical error: Almost each participant at the marathon (A) / was exhausted due to the (B) / intensely humid weather conditions. (C) / No error (D)
opts: Almost each participant at the marathon
questions.ansText: Almost each participant at the marathon
questions.why: Words like 'almost', 'nearly', and 'approximately' can only be paired with 'Every', never with 'Each'. It must be 'Almost every participant'.

questions.q:
**Direction: Read the passage carefully and answer the question that follows.**

Recently, the CEO of a large multinational asked whether the upcoming visit of the United States Trade Representative to India could result in tariff rates returning to 18%. Such conversations reflect the extent to which trade negotiations are often viewed strictly through the prism of headline tariff numbers. Yet, in practice, the more significant determinants of market access and competitiveness frequently lie elsewhere. For decades, trade diplomacy revolved around tariffs. Governments negotiated reductions in import duties, and success was measured in percentage points shaved off customs rates. However, since the establishment of the World Trade Organization (WTO) in 1995, average tariff rates have fallen by nearly half, yet governments have not abandoned protectionism. As tariffs declined, non-tariff barriers (NTBs) surged. Today, NTBs affect around 90% of global trade - a sixfold increase over the past three decades.

NTBs are the regulations, certifications, licensing rules, and product requirements that goods must meet before entering a market. More than half of the 20,000 global product and safety regulations introduced over the past 70 years have emerged since 2000. Among major economies, the European Union (EU) is the most extensive user of these regulatory tools, with non-tariff measures covering roughly 94% of imports entering the EU, compared with about 77% in the U.S. and nearly 45% in India. The EU has built an expansive regulatory architecture focused on environmental rules, chemical safety, and climate-related policies such as the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism and the Deforestation Regulation. Conversely, American NTBs are driven by strategic competition and security concerns, aggressively using export controls and restrictions on semiconductors, AI chips, and advanced computing hardware to limit rivals' access to critical tech supply chains.

India has traditionally relied more on tariffs, but this is changing. To boost domestic manufacturing, New Delhi is expanding quality regulations on imports of electronics and chemicals. India's own Free Trade Agreement (FTA) record makes the point sharply. Despite agreements existing on paper, India's FTA utilisation rate is about 25%, compared with 70%-80% for developed economies. Preferential tariff utilisation among Indian businesses for the ASEAN agreement remains below 50% because NTBs make claiming these benefits commercially impractical. Indonesian registration requirements restrict Indian pharmaceutical exports, while Thai customs procedures force gem exporters to reroute shipments through Hong Kong. Similarly, despite a 2011 FTA with Japan, Indian pharma exports remain negligible because market approvals can take up to seven years. However, India's newer agreements signal a genuine shift. The UAE Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement and the India-EFTA pact explicitly mandate automatic recognition of medicines approved by major regulators and require mutual acceptance of laboratory testing to eliminate duplicate compliance costs, making NTB reduction a legally binding obligation for the first time.

What is the central theme of the passage?
opts: The complete failure of the World Trade Organization in regulating international commerce.
The shift in global trade protectionism from traditional tariffs to complex non-tariff barriers.
The environmental regulations imposed by the EU to stop deforestation in Asian countries.
The rapid growth of the Indian pharmaceutical industry in Japan and ASEAN nations.
questions.ansText: The shift in global trade protectionism from traditional tariffs to complex non-tariff barriers.
questions.why: The passage revolves around the argument that while tariffs have fallen globally, countries have adopted complex non-tariff barriers (NTBs) as the new tools of trade protectionism.

As tariffs declined, non-tariff barriers (NTBs) surged. Today, NTBs affect around 90% of global trade - a sixfold increase over the past three decades.

NTBs are the regulations, certifications, licensing rules, and product requirements that goods must meet before entering a market. More than half of the 20,000 global product and safety regulations introduced over the past 70 years have emerged since 2000. Among major economies, the European Union (EU) is the most extensive user of these regulatory tools, with non-tariff measures covering roughly 94% of imports entering the EU, compared with about 77% in the U.S. and nearly 45% in India. The EU has built an expansive regulatory architecture focused on environmental rules, chemical safety, and climate-related policies such as the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism and the Deforestation Regulation. Conversely, American NTBs are driven by strategic competition and security concerns, aggressively using export controls and restrictions on semiconductors, AI chips, and advanced computing hardware to limit rivals' access to critical tech supply chains.

India has traditionally relied more on tariffs, but this is changing. To boost domestic manufacturing, New Delhi is expanding quality regulations on imports of electronics and chemicals. India's own Free Trade Agreement (FTA) record makes the point sharply. Despite agreements existing on paper, India's FTA utilisation rate is about 25%, compared with 70%-80% for developed economies. Preferential tariff utilisation among Indian businesses for the ASEAN agreement remains below 50% because NTBs make claiming these benefits commercially impractical. Indonesian registration requirements restrict Indian pharmaceutical exports, while Thai customs procedures force gem exporters to reroute shipments through Hong Kong. Similarly, despite a 2011 FTA with Japan, Indian pharma exports remain negligible because market approvals can take up to seven years. However, India's newer agreements signal a genuine shift. The UAE Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement and the India-EFTA pact explicitly mandate automatic recognition of medicines approved by major regulators and require mutual acceptance of laboratory testing to eliminate duplicate compliance costs, making NTB reduction a legally binding obligation for the first time.

questions.why: The author is critical of the narrow focus on tariffs, stating that viewing trade strictly through this prism misses the 'more significant determinants' (NTBs) that actually affect market access.
